title: Elasticity and Mechanical Properties of Solids
short_intro: Elasticity is the property of a body by virtue of which it tends to regain its original shape and size after the removal of the deforming force. Hooke's law governs the linear elastic regime where stress is directly proportional to strain.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Stress, strain, Hooke's law, elastic moduli (Young's, Bulk, Rigidity), Poisson's ratio, and elementary strain energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Interatomic forces, relation between elastic constants, twisting couple of a cylinder, bending of beams, and energy stored per unit volume under complex loading.

concept_notes.heading: Stress and Strain Fundamentals
bullets: Stress is the restoring force per unit area set up inside a deformed body, measured in N/m² or Pascal (Pa).
Normal stress acts perpendicular to the surface (tensile or compressive), while tangential or shearing stress acts parallel to the surface.
Strain is a dimensionless quantity representing fractional change in dimensions; longitudinal strain is ΔL/L, volumetric strain is ΔV/V, and shearing strain is angular displacement θ.

concept_notes.heading: Hooke's Law and Elastic Moduli
bullets: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain, defining the modulus of elasticity E = Stress / Strain.
Young's modulus (Y) relates longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain for tensile or compressive loading.
Bulk modulus (K) relates normal stress (pressure change) to volumetric strain, and its reciprocal is compressibility.

concept_notes.heading: Rigidity Modulus and Poisson's Ratio
bullets: Rigidity modulus (η) is the ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain, relevant only to shape changes in solids.
Poisson's ratio (σ) is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial tension, theoretically bounded between -1.0 and 0.5.
For isotropic materials, the practical upper limit of Poisson's ratio is 0.5 (incompressibility).

concept_notes.heading: Elastic Potential Energy
bullets: Work done in deforming an elastic body is stored as elastic potential energy within the material.
Energy stored per unit volume is given by u = (1/2) × Stress × Strain.
Total elastic potential energy for a stretched wire of length L and cross-sectional area A is U = (1/2) × (Y A / L) × (ΔL)².

derivations.title: Work Done in Stretching a Wire
derivations.conditions: Within elastic limit, linear Hooke's law regime
steps: Let a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A be stretched by an infinitesimal amount dx under a stretching force F.
The work done for this small displacement is dW = F dx.
Substituting F = (Y A x) / L from Hooke's law, integrate dW from x = 0 to x = ΔL.
W = int_{0}^{Delta L}  rac{YA x}{L} dx =  rac{YA}{L} left[ rac{x^2}{2}ight]_{0}^{Delta L} =  rac{1}{2}  rac{YA (Delta L)^2}{L}.

derivations.title: Relation between Elastic Constants (Y, K, and η)
steps: Express Young's modulus in terms of Bulk modulus K and rigidity modulus η using strain components under triaxial loading.
The fundamental relations connecting elastic constants are Y = 9Kη / (3K + η) and Y = 2η(1 + σ).
Eliminate Poisson's ratio (σ) to establish the direct thermodynamic identity among Y, K, and η.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stress-Strain Curve for a Metallic Wire
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph with tensile strain on the x-axis and tensile stress on the y-axis, showing proportionality limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength point, and fracture point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Region up to yield point is elastic; beyond yield point, plastic deformation occurs, ending in necking and fracture.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identifying ultimate tensile strength and distinguishing ductile from brittle materials.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing two parallel wires (experimental and reference) loaded with weights, equipped with a spirit level and micrometer screw.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Eliminates thermal expansion errors by using a reference wire while measuring minute elongations ΔL corresponding to applied load F.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Determining Young's modulus of a metallic wire in laboratory settings.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hysteresis Loop for Cyclic Loading
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Loading and unloading stress-strain curves forming a closed loop during cyclic elastic-plastic deformation.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed by the loop represents mechanical energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Understanding damping capacity and energy loss in vibrating mechanical structures.

solved_numericals.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 mm² is stretched by 2 mm. If Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m², calculate the tension developed in the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 2 m, A = 1 mm² = 1 × 10&sup-;&sup6; m², ΔL = 2 mm = 2 × 10&sup-;³ m, Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
Apply Young's modulus formula: F = (Y A ΔL) / L.

solved_numericals.question: Find the elastic potential energy stored in a steel wire of length 4 m and cross-sectional area 0.5 cm² when stretched by 1 mm. Given Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m².
solution_steps: Convert units: L = 4 m, A = 0.5 cm² = 0.5 × 10&sup-;&sup4; m², ΔL = 1 × 10&sup-;³ m.
Use energy formula: U = (1/2) × (Y A / L) × (ΔL)².

solved_numericals.question: For a given isotropic material, the Young's modulus is 2.4 times its rigidity modulus. Calculate the Poisson's ratio of the material.
solution_steps: Use the relation between Young's modulus and rigidity modulus: Y = 2η(1 + σ).
Substitute the condition into the relation: 2.4 η = 2η(1 + σ).
Cancel η and solve for σ: 1.2 = 1 + σ, which yields σ = 0.2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Hooke's law is strictly valid only within the proportional limit of the stress-strain curve.
Materials are assumed to be perfectly isotropic and homogeneous unless specified otherwise.
Deformations are assumed to be infinitesimally small so that geometrical non-linearities can be neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Rubber is less elastic than steel because it stretches more easily.
common_misconceptions.correct: Steel is more elastic than rubber because its Young's modulus is significantly higher, meaning it requires more stress to produce a given strain.
common_misconceptions.why: Elasticity measures resistance to deformation (modulus), not the maximum possible elongation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio can take any positive value up to infinity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Poisson's ratio for stable isotropic solids is theoretically restricted between -1.0 and 0.5.
common_misconceptions.why: Values outside this range would violate thermodynamic stability conditions requiring positive bulk and shear moduli.

quick_revision: Modulus of elasticity has the same dimensional formula and SI unit as stress (Pa).
Poisson's ratio is dimensionless and has no units.
Energy density stored in a stretched medium is half the product of stress and strain.
Bulk modulus for an incompressible liquid is infinity.
